A 2024 clinical report describes two cases of contact urticaria—hives after skin contact—from phenoxyethanol in other cosmetics. A case report documents a possible reaction, not how frequently it occurs or that either serum caused it.

The EU Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety concluded that phenoxyethanol is safe as a cosmetic preservative up to 1.0% under its assessment. That is not a guarantee of individual tolerance or an assay of these US products.

practicalDifferences.title: Compare equal bottle sizes
practicalDifferences.text: Both records describe 30 mL. The table shows dated prices and their cost per mL. A lower price measures cost, not product quality.

practicalDifferences.title: Check the version’s own directions
practicalDifferences.text: Do not transfer one product’s compatibility guidance to the other. Read the manufacturer’s current instructions for the specific version you intend to use.

comparisons.limitations: The catalog shows selected label peptides, not complete formulas. Individual concentrations may be undisclosed. No independent head-to-head effectiveness or individual tolerance is established here. This editorial draft awaits human review.

decisionNotes.title: If your question is about cost
decisionNotes.text: Compare the same bottle size in the table, with each observation date. Multi-Peptide + HA has the lower recorded cost here; that does not measure the extra benefit of copper.

decisionNotes.title: If your question is about adding copper
decisionNotes.text: Inspect the exact copper name and the complete current directions. We cannot use label presence to promise an extra visible result or to predict your skin’s reaction.

questions.question: Is the copper version just the same serum with one extra ingredient?
questions.answer: These selected lists cannot establish that the complete formulas differ by only one ingredient. Read both full manufacturer lists before treating them as interchangeable.

questions.question: Does 1% copper mean fewer peptides than the HA version?
questions.answer: No. A disclosed percentage and an ingredient count answer different questions. The records do not disclose a separate amount of every selected peptide in either serum.

comparisons.title: NIOD CAIS3 vs. The Ordinary copper peptide serum
comparisons.editorialSummary: Compare NIOD CAIS3 and The Ordinary copper serum with a draft critical review of ingredient benefits, documented reactions, long-term evidence gaps and price limitations. Scientific evidence is kept separate from label claims.
comparisons.documentedDifferences: NIOD lists Tripeptide-1 Copper Acetate; The Ordinary lists Copper Tripeptide-1. These exact label names are retained without asserting molecular or clinical equivalence. The Ordinary also lists Acetyl Hexapeptide-8; NIOD lists Tripeptide-29. The ingredient selections shown here are incomplete.
comparisons.limitations: Selected peptides and two additional preservative label entries were checked, not an exhaustive toxicological assessment of every ingredient. The inspected sources do not establish head-to-head outcomes or years of safety for these finished formulas. NIOD’s 30 mL price remains unverified. Editorial and qualified scientific review are pending.
comparisons.buyerQuestion: Are these copper serums interchangeable, and what differences can I actually verify?

practicalDifferences.title: Start with the exact copper name
practicalDifferences.text: NIOD lists Tripeptide-1 Copper Acetate; The Ordinary lists Copper Tripeptide-1. The word copper alone does not establish identical ingredients or performance.

practicalDifferences.title: Other selected peptides also differ
practicalDifferences.text: NIOD lists Tripeptide-29 and Acetyl Tetrapeptide-2; The Ordinary lists Acetyl Hexapeptide-8 and palmitoyl peptides. Open the explanations to understand the names; do not treat the count as a quality score.

practicalDifferences.title: Leave the cost question open
practicalDifferences.text: The NIOD record is for 30 mL. A price for a different size would produce a misleading comparison, so no NIOD price per mL or cost winner is shown.

decisionNotes.title: If your question is whether the copper names are equivalent
decisionNotes.text: The exact names differ in the recorded labels. This comparison preserves them separately rather than treating both as the same ingredient.

decisionNotes.title: If you are comparing value
decisionNotes.text: The NIOD record describes 30 mL, but the catalog has no verified price for that variant. Use a current size-specific retailer price in the calculator; do not substitute a 15 mL price.

questions.question: Does NIOD’s 1:1 mean the same as The Ordinary’s 1%?
questions.answer: NIOD describes two components in its technology; The Ordinary’s name includes a copper-peptide percentage. These different disclosures do not establish identical individual ingredient amounts.

questions.question: Can this page tell me which copper serum works better?
questions.answer: No. It compares selected label facts and cost information where verified. It does not establish comparative results, individual tolerance or equivalent copper forms.

questions.question: Does a phenoxyethanol case report mean I should reject both serums?
questions.answer: Not on that evidence alone. The cases concern other cosmetics and do not give a reaction rate for these products. The SCCS safety conclusion has defined use conditions and does not guarantee individual tolerance. A known ingredient allergy is a separate reason to discuss suitable alternatives with your clinician.

researchContext.text: An Argireline trial in 60 Chinese participants over four weeks reported improvements in eye-area wrinkle measures relative to placebo. The Ordinary lists Acetyl Hexapeptide-8, but that label entry does not make its complete serum the studied treatment. The abstract does not identify either compared copper serum as the tested product. We use this study to explain the limits of transferring ingredient research, not to select a winner.

evaluations.title: Before you buy: benefits, risks and the evidence gaps
evaluations.summary: The research inspected does not establish that either finished serum works better or is safer. There is short-term ingredient evidence, documented preservative reactions in other cosmetics, and safety assessments with defined limits. These are reasons to ask better questions, not to declare either formula harmful.

sections.title: Benefits: ingredient evidence is not a product promise
sections.conclusion: A benefit signal exists for Argireline; superiority of either copper serum is not established here.

paragraphs.text: A randomized placebo-controlled Argireline study in 60 Chinese participants reported improvement in eye-area wrinkle measures after four weeks. It did not identify these two retail serums as the tested treatment.

A separate laboratory study on human cadaver and guinea-pig skin found limited penetration of acetyl hexapeptide-8 from its tested emulsion. This was a 24-hour experiment, not a clinical wrinkle trial; it cannot prove these serums work or do not work.

For this purchase, ingredient research is a starting point. We have not established a head-to-head clinical result for NIOD versus The Ordinary. Do not pay extra on the assumption that a more expensive copper serum has proven superior results.

sections.title: Risks: look beyond the peptide
sections.conclusion: Preservative reactions are documented, but their likelihood in these serums is unknown.

paragraphs.text: A 2024 clinical report describes two cases of contact urticaria—hives after skin contact—from phenoxyethanol in other cosmetics. A case report documents a possible reaction, not how frequently it occurs or that either serum caused it.

The EU Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety concluded that phenoxyethanol is safe as a cosmetic preservative up to 1.0% under its assessment. That is not a guarantee of individual tolerance or an assay of these US products.

The label check below identifies phenoxyethanol in both formulas. If you have a confirmed allergy to it, that is a concrete reason to discuss alternatives with your clinician. Ingredient presence alone cannot diagnose an allergy or establish that one of these products is riskier.

The 2025 Acetyl Hexapeptide-8 safety assessment reaches a favorable conclusion up to 0.005%, with insufficient data above that amount. This does not establish harm above it or certify a serum with an unverified pure-peptide concentration.

sections.title: Long-term use: a safety assessment has boundaries
sections.conclusion: Neither a short trial nor an ingredient assessment establishes years of safety for these complete formulas.

paragraphs.text: The CIR assessment includes Copper Tripeptide-1 and specified related peptides and concludes safe use under the practices and concentrations it reviewed. Its scope does not automatically cover every copper-named ingredient or either complete serum.

The inspected CIR report notes gaps in reproductive/developmental toxicity and carcinogenicity data for its reviewed group, while still reaching its scoped safe-use conclusion. A missing dataset is not evidence that these products cause those harms.

This review does not establish long-term harm or long-term safety for either finished serum. We have not performed an exhaustive search or a clinical safety review. We also do not transfer injection, ingestion or microneedling findings to normal cosmetic application on intact skin.

sections.title: Value: what would justify paying more?
sections.conclusion: A price premium is not evidence of a health or performance advantage.

paragraphs.text: The inspected studies and safety assessments do not compare the two finished products. They cannot establish that paying more buys better wrinkle reduction, lower allergy risk or greater long-term safety.

Our catalog still lacks a verified price for NIOD’s 30 mL variant, so we cannot calculate a fair cost difference yet. Compare the exact size and current price separately from the scientific evidence. Personal format preferences may matter, but we have not tested texture or wear.

evaluations.labelContext: The current US ingredient lists for both products name Phenoxyethanol and Chlorphenesin. These are additional label checks, not additions to our selected-peptide list. Individual preservative concentrations are not given in the inspected lists. The academic phenoxyethanol case report concerns different cosmetics; it is not an adverse-event report for these two serums. NIOD also advertises product tests with 31–32 people over 4–12 weeks. We have not assessed their full protocols or an independently published head-to-head result; these brand-reported claims are separate from the academic evidence above.

evaluations.title: Before you buy: does adding copper justify the difference?
evaluations.summary: The labels and recorded prices show a purchasing difference. The selected research does not establish extra benefit or better tolerance from the copper version. Both full formulas need to be considered, not just their peptide names.

sections.title: Benefits: neither bottle inherits an ingredient result
sections.conclusion: A short ingredient trial does not establish which complete serum works better.

paragraphs.text: A four-week randomized placebo-controlled Argireline trial enrolled 60 Chinese participants. It reported improvements in eye-area wrinkle measures; the abstract does not identify either compared retail serum as its treatment.
Both recorded labels include Acetyl Hexapeptide-8. That shared name does not transfer the trial result to either formula or demonstrate an advantage from adding copper.

sections.title: Precautions: ingredient assessments have concentration limits
sections.conclusion: The safety assessment cannot certify either finished serum or predict your tolerance.

paragraphs.text: The 2025 Acetyl Hexapeptide-8 safety assessment reaches a favorable conclusion up to 0.005%, with insufficient data above that amount. This does not establish harm above it or certify a serum with an unverified pure-peptide concentration.
Neither label check establishes the separate pure amount of Acetyl Hexapeptide-8. Do not compare a commercial blend’s headline percentage directly with the assessment’s pure-ingredient concentration.

sections.title: Long-term evidence: keep the reviewed scope visible
sections.conclusion: A scoped cosmetic assessment is not years of testing these complete formulas.

paragraphs.text: The 2018 safety assessment covers specified peptide identities, uses and concentrations, including Copper Tripeptide-1 and the selected palmitoyl peptides it names. Its favorable conclusion applies within that reviewed scope.
This selected-source review does not establish comparative long-term safety, nor does a missing finished-product study demonstrate that either serum causes harm.

sections.title: Value: price answers the cost question
sections.conclusion: The lower recorded cost is not a clinical performance ranking.

paragraphs.text: Use the dated, equal-size prices in Ingredients & price. The lower recorded cost of Multi-Peptide + HA does not measure the additional benefit, if any, of the copper version. Texture and wear have not been tested by Peptivelo.

evaluations.labelContext: The recorded US labels name Acetyl Hexapeptide-8 in both serums and Copper Tripeptide-1 in the copper version. The selected lists are incomplete; they do not establish that the full formulas differ only by copper. Individual peptide amounts are not independently assayed. Directions may vary by product and reformulation.
